purpose: Record what each shell matches for the `case` patterns a real workflow writes, so the frontend's pattern model is checked against a measurement rather than against a reading of the specification.
note: The word is base64 so a newline survives the file, the script is the whole program each shell is given, and the answer is an ASCII token so nothing is lost to a text decode. Agreement across the columns is not evidence that a pattern does what it was written to do: `newline-via-command-substitution` answers the same in all four shells and is wrong in all four, because command substitution strips the newline the guard was built to hold; `caret-set-member` answers the same by two opposite rules, and the same pattern against a different word is where they part. A corpus that only asked whether the shells agree would pass both in silence. A shell that refuses the pattern is recorded as `ERROR` and nothing more: the message names the interpreter's own path and the script's name, neither of which is a property of the pattern. Program names are not semantic versions: observed dash builds match one of two complete profiles across all 45 cases, never a convenient answer selected case by case.
